answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering node in a particular per-layer TE network; it represents a node participating in that layer's TE topology.
answers.example: ROADM R1 in the OTN layer network.
answers.relations: It is part of i.tetopo. Its i.tp termination points, i.ttp tunnel heads, i.tcep connection endpoints, and i.cmatrix switching constraints may be associated with it; i.telink objects run between such nodes.

answers.gloss: A termination point on a TE node at which a TE link terminates.
answers.example: The termination point on R1 facing R2 for the R1-R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It is owned by or located on i.tenode and terminates i.telink. It is a topology/link endpoint, not specifically a service-access endpoint or tunnel head.

answers.gloss: The supporting relationship by which a client-layer termination point is supported by a server-layer termination point.
answers.example: An OTN termination point supported by an optical-layer termination point at R1.
answers.relations: It expresses inter-layer adaptation/support involving i.tp objects. In this model it denotes the support relationship, rather than merely another ordinary TP.

answers.gloss: The point at which a TE tunnel originates or terminates—a tunnel trail head.
answers.example: The A1 trail head of the A1-A3 ODU2 tunnel.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and originates or terminates i.tunnel. It is specifically a tunnel endpoint; this model does not inherently define it as an externally exposed service-access point.

answers.gloss: An end-to-end traffic-engineered tunnel that realizes connectivity for a service.
answers.example: The A1-A3 ODU2 TE tunnel.
answers.relations: It runs between i.ttp tunnel heads, traverses i.tetopo resources, has internal/node-local i.tcep endpoints, and may be labelled by i.otnlabel. It is the TE realization construct, rather than merely an abstract customer request.

answers.gloss: An OTN TE label expressing the tributary-slot multiplexing structure used for carriage.
answers.example: The TS/TPN selection for carrying an ODU2 within an OTU4.
answers.relations: It labels i.tunnel and captures the relevant OTN multiplex allocation/structure. Its semantics are concrete tributary-slot/TPN label information, not just a generic statement of layer type.

answers.gloss: The matrix of internal connectivity that a node permits.
answers.example: R2's matrix specifying which ingress and egress termination points may be cross-connected.
answers.relations: It is associated with i.tenode and constrains permissible internal switching/cross-connect connectivity among the node's terminations.

answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering link representing a topological adjacency between TE nodes in one layer network.
answers.example: The R1-R2 TE link.
answers.relations: It is between i.tenode objects, is terminated by their i.tp objects, and is contained in i.tetopo.

answers.gloss: A traffic-engineering network/topology for one particular layer.
answers.example: The OTN layer network containing R1, R2, R3, and their OTN TE links.
answers.relations: It contains i.tenode and i.telink objects and provides the topology over which i.tunnel is realized. This concept is per-layer, not one undifferentiated multi-layer domain object.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a tunnel connection within a node.
answers.example: The connection endpoint for the A1-A3 tunnel on R1.
answers.relations: It is on i.tenode and is part of i.tunnel. It represents a tunnel/connection endpoint internal to the network model, distinct from an ordinary link-termination i.tp and from the tunnel trail-head i.ttp.

answers.gloss: A forwarding or switching node in the domain's single multi-layer topology. It may participate in multiple layer views rather than being intrinsically scoped to only one layer.
answers.example: ROADM R1 in the OTN-over-optical domain.
answers.relations: It is part of t.topo. Its edge points t.ltp, service access points t.sip, connection endpoints t.cep, adaptation links t.translink, and switching rule groups t.nrg may be associated with it; t.link objects connect nodes.

answers.gloss: A node-owned edge point at which a topological link terminates.
answers.example: The R1 edge point facing R2 on the R1-R2 link.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and terminates t.link. This model does not explicitly state that an LTP contains layer-specific t.cep objects; t.cep is modeled separately as a connection endpoint on a node.

answers.gloss: A link expressing adaptation between client and server layers within a node.
answers.example: The OTU4-to-ODU2 adaptation at R1.
answers.relations: It is at t.node and expresses adaptation involving the multiplex/layer structure represented by t.lpq. The supplied model does not enumerate separate endpoint objects for the transitional link.

answers.gloss: An externally exposed point through which a client service accesses the network.
answers.example: The ODU2 client hand-off at A1.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and provides access to t.cs. No direct containment or identity relation to t.ltp or t.cep is asserted in this model; it is a service-access abstraction rather than inherently a tunnel trail head.

answers.gloss: An end-to-end connectivity service across the network.
answers.example: The requested A1-to-A3 ODU2 service.
answers.relations: It uses t.sip access points, has t.cep connection endpoints, and is carried over t.topo. It denotes the service connectivity abstraction, not a separately modeled TE tunnel or computed path that realizes the request.

answers.gloss: A qualifier expressing the layer and multiplexing structure of a signal.
answers.example: ODU2 mapped into an OTU4 server signal.
answers.relations: It qualifies t.cs and is involved in the adaptation expressed by t.translink. The concept does not identify a concrete tributary-slot or TPN allocation in the supplied model.

answers.gloss: A node rule group containing constraints on which ports may be internally cross-connected.
answers.example: The permitted ingress-to-egress cross-connect rules on R2.
answers.relations: It is associated with t.node and constrains internal switching. The model describes a rule group and does not assert that one instance must be the complete connectivity matrix for the entire node.

answers.gloss: A topological adjacency between two nodes in the domain topology.
answers.example: The R1-R2 link.
answers.relations: It runs between t.node objects, is terminated by node-owned t.ltp objects, and is contained in t.topo. Because t.topo is multi-layer, the concept is not intrinsically restricted here to a separate per-layer topology object.

answers.gloss: The single multi-layer topology describing the managed domain.
answers.example: The OTN-over-optical topology containing the transport and optical resources.
answers.relations: It contains t.node and t.link objects and carries t.cs. Unlike a per-layer topology, one t.topo may represent the combined multi-layer domain.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a service connection within a node.
answers.example: The endpoint for the A1-A3 service on R1.
answers.relations: It is on t.node and part of t.cs. This model does not state that it is contained by t.ltp or that a topological t.link terminates on it; link termination belongs to t.ltp.

proposals.rationale: Both denote a node-owned topology edge point on which the corresponding topological link terminates; neither is inherently a service-access point or tunnel head.
Both express an intra-node client/server inter-layer adaptation or support relationship. The representations differ in naming and explicit endpoints, but their modeled role is the same.
Both encode the permissible internal cross-connects among a node's terminations. TAPI packages these constraints as a rule group, whereas the IETF concept presents them as a connectivity matrix.

Both are topological adjacencies between forwarding/TE nodes and terminate on the corresponding node-owned termination points. The remaining topology-layer scoping difference belongs mainly to their containers.
Both are node-local endpoints of the end-to-end connection or tunnel construct and are distinct from ordinary link-termination points.

Test whether the abstract connectivity service and the TE tunnel realization preserve endpoint identity, connectivity, and capacity, or whether service-versus-realization semantics make them false cognates.
Test whether a generic layer/multiplex qualifier and a concrete tributary-slot/TPN allocation preserve multiplex structure and capacity under translation.
